title: Active, Passive, Causative and Related Constructions
orientation: Voice helps a writer choose what to put first and what to leave in the background. A technician repaired the scanner begins with the technician; the scanner was repaired begins with the scanner and may leave the technician unnamed. Neither form is automatically clearer or more formal. Its usefulness depends on what the reader already knows and which information matters. Today you will build passives accurately, interpret reporting and get-passives, and distinguish them from causative constructions such as having a scanner repaired. You will also identify restrictions: a change of voice is possible only where the lexical pattern and intended meaning support it. Review verb phrases, objects, aspect and modality first. During transformation, preserve time, negation, modal strength, agents when relevant and relationships such as who received what. A mechanically correct-looking formula can still change the original claim.
outcomes: Build be-passives with appropriate tense, aspect and modal auxiliaries.
Choose an agentless, reporting, get- or double-object passive in context.
Use have, get, make, let and help with their own complement patterns.
Distinguish an active intransitive change of state from a passive.
Explain lexical and discourse restrictions on meaning-preserving transformations.

modules.title: Building the passive verb phrase
modules.definition: A canonical be-passive uses a form of be plus a lexical past participle and normally presents as subject an element corresponding to an object in a related active clause.
foundation: Compare The technician repairs the scanner with The scanner is repaired by the technician. The scanner is the object in the active and the subject in the passive. Be supplies the finite present form, and repaired is a participle. The subject of a passive is therefore not necessarily the performer of an action. Form a negative or a question through the first auxiliary: The scanner is not repaired here; Is the scanner repaired here? A by-phrase can identify the agent, but it is often omitted when unknown, obvious or unimportant.
intermediate: Preserve tense and aspect through the auxiliary chain. Active is repairing corresponds to passive is being repaired; was repairing corresponds to was being repaired. Has repaired corresponds to has been repaired; had repaired to had been repaired. A modal comes before base be: can be repaired. A modal perfect uses have been: must have been repaired. Future perfect reference can use will have been repaired. To-infinitives can likewise be passive: to be repaired; a perfect passive infinitive is to have been repaired. The lexical participle remains repaired through these changes; the preceding auxiliaries carry the grammatical distinctions.
advanced: The sequence has been being repaired is grammatically available for a perfect-progressive passive, but it is uncommon and often cumbersome. In ordinary writing, an active clause such as technicians have been repairing it, or a suitably contextual recast, is often easier to process. Avoid calling a difficult but possible combination impossible. Conversely, do not lose duration by replacing has been being repaired for a month with was repaired a month ago: the latter presents a different time relationship. Choose a recast that preserves what is known about continuation or completion.
expert: Not every sequence of be plus a participial-looking word has a uniquely verbal passive analysis. The door was closed at six can report the closing event or describe the resulting state, depending on context. A clear agent phrase or an event-focused progressive can support a verbal reading, while a contrast of states can support an adjectival reading. Individual diagnostics have limits because words can belong to more than one construction. In analysis, describe the reading actually licensed by the discourse rather than assigning a label from the surface ending alone. In transformation, check the original verb's complements before selecting a new subject.

patterns.meaning: A basic passive; be carries tense and agreement.

patterns.form: modal + be / modal + have been + past participle
patterns.meaning: Simple or perfect passive under a modal.

patterns.form: to be / to have been + past participle

examples.sentence: The labels are checked before dispatch.
examples.analysis: Present passive describes the checking procedure; labels is the grammatical subject.

examples.sentence: The labels were being checked when the power failed.
examples.analysis: Past progressive passive presents checking as in progress at the interruption.

examples.sentence: The labels must have been checked before dispatch.
examples.analysis: The modal-perfect passive can express a deduction in an evidential context; context determines the modal reading.

contrasts.a: The clerk has stamped the form.
contrasts.b: The form has been stamped by the clerk.
contrasts.note: Both grammatical; the passive preserves the perfect and changes the information placed first.

exceptions: Perfect-progressive passives exist but are uncommon: the bridge has been being inspected. Prefer a clear recast without pretending that the form is universally ungrammatical. Be plus participle can also describe a state.

mistakes.reason: The lexical verb requires its participle written after passive be.

mistakes.problem: The form is being checked yesterday. [completed yesterday]
mistakes.reason: Use a past form for the explicitly completed earlier event; preserve an ongoing reading only if the context supplies one.

glossary.definition: A grammatical contrast affecting how participants are expressed in a clause.
glossary.example: The clerk signed it / It was signed by the clerk.

glossary.definition: The participant carrying out an action, when the event has such a participant.
glossary.example: In The file was signed by Noor, Noor is the agent.

modules.title: Agents, reporting, get-passives and two-object verbs
modules.definition: Passive constructions can background an agent, report a claim or promote different objects, while get-passives often present a dynamic event in a more conversational register.
foundation: An agentless passive is useful when the affected item is the continuing topic: The scanner arrived yesterday. It was installed this morning. Omitting an unknown agent avoids inventing one. It can also obscure responsibility, so the omission should serve the reader's purpose. A known, important agent may belong in a by-phrase: The decision was overturned by the appeal panel. Active and passive versions organise information differently; neither voice is a universal rule for professional writing. Some passive clauses describe states rather than obvious deliberate actions, so agent is not always the best semantic label for every by-phrase.
intermediate: Reporting passives include It is believed that the bridge is safe and The bridge is believed to be safe. The first uses impersonal it and a content clause; the second places bridge first with an infinitival complement. For an event earlier than the reporting belief, use a perfect infinitive where appropriate: The bridge is believed to have opened in 1980. The construction attributes a belief; it does not guarantee the proposition is true. Keep the source if it matters: The bridge is believed by local historians to have opened in 1980 is more informative than an entirely unattributed report.
advanced: With suitable two-object verbs, either recipient or transferred item can become passive subject: The charity gave the school a printer; The school was given a printer; A printer was given to the school. The alternatives are not unlimited for every verb. Explain takes the pattern explain something to someone in the intended sense; The rule was explained to her follows that pattern, whereas She was explained the rule is not the ordinary standard counterpart. Learn the lexical pattern, not just an abstract two-object formula. Different dialects and particular verbs also differ in their preferred passive alternatives.
expert: A get-passive uses get plus a participle: The parcel got damaged. It is especially common in conversation and typically foregrounds an event or the affected participant. It is not confined to bad outcomes: She got promoted reports a desirable event in many contexts. Get does not by itself prove that the subject caused or deserved the outcome. Adding a reflexive, as in He got himself locked out, can suggest responsibility, but context still matters. A state such as The answer is known does not automatically have a natural equivalent with get. Keep meaning and register in view when choosing between be, get and an active clause.

patterns.meaning: Reports an attributed proposition with impersonal it.
Puts a participant in the reported proposition first.
Possible with suitable ditransitive verbs such as give.

examples.sentence: The museum was given a complete catalogue.
examples.analysis: Museum is the recipient promoted from a give construction.

examples.sentence: The manuscript is thought to have survived the fire.
examples.analysis: The perfect infinitive places survival before the present attribution of belief.

examples.sentence: The trainee got promoted after the trial period.
examples.analysis: Get-passive describes an event; a negative outcome is not required.

contrasts.a: The school was given a printer.
contrasts.b: A printer was given to the school.
contrasts.note: Both grammatical for the same transfer in context; they foreground different participants.

exceptions: Get-passives can report positive events and need not imply fault. Not all verbs allow both double-object/passive alternatives: lexical complementation must be checked.

mistakes.repair: The rule was explained to her.
mistakes.reason: The intended explain pattern takes the rule as object and to her as recipient phrase.

mistakes.problem: The bridge is believed to opened in 1980.
mistakes.repair: The bridge is believed to have opened in 1980.
mistakes.reason: Use a perfect infinitive to express the earlier opening under the present reporting verb.

glossary.definition: A passive without an expressed agent phrase.
A passive construction attributing a report, belief or judgement.
glossary.example: The files are believed to be intact.

modules.title: Causatives and their complement patterns
modules.definition: Causative constructions express arranging, causing or enabling another action, but have, get, make, let and help differ in grammar and in the kind of involvement they commonly convey.
foundation: Have something done commonly describes arranging for someone else to act: We had the scanner repaired. The object scanner is followed by the participle repaired; the sentence does not say that we personally repaired it. Get something done can describe arranging or achieving a similar result: We got the scanner repaired before Monday. Here get is not simply an interchangeable auxiliary in every context. A causative sentence has its own subject and participant structure, so converting I repaired the scanner into I had the scanner repaired normally changes who performed or arranged the work.
intermediate: Have can also introduce a person and a bare infinitive: I had the technician check the wiring. Get commonly uses a person plus to-infinitive: I got the technician to check the wiring. In a suitable context it can suggest persuasion or successfully arranging cooperation. Make plus a person and a bare infinitive often expresses causing or compelling an action: The delay made us reconsider. Let normally expresses permission: The supervisor let us leave. Help accepts a bare or to-infinitive: She helped me check it; she helped me to check it. These patterns should be learned alongside their typical meanings.
advanced: Passive make restores to: We were made to wait. In the permission meaning of let, be allowed to is the ordinary passive alternative: We were allowed to leave, rather than mechanically producing were let to leave. Some other uses of let, such as letting property or the fixed expression be let go, behave differently. Do not generalise a restriction on one meaning to every occurrence of a word. Help him to leave and help him leave are both standard; choosing one does not justify marking the other wrong. Register and local preference can affect frequency without changing grammaticality.
expert: Have plus object plus participle is not always an arranged service. We had our equipment stolen ordinarily reports an adverse experience, not an instruction to steal it. Context distinguishes that reading from a causative arrangement. Similarly, We had visitors waiting outside uses an -ing complement and can describe an experience or an ongoing state brought about by circumstances. The order of have and an object matters: We had repaired the scanner is past perfect, whereas We had the scanner repaired is the object-plus-participle construction. Analyse the complete verb phrase before inferring agency, time or responsibility. A meaningful transformation must preserve these distinctions rather than merely reproduce a familiar sequence.

patterns.meaning: Often an arranged service or achieved result; context can supply an adverse-experience reading.

patterns.form: have + person + bare infinitive / get + person + to-infinitive
patterns.meaning: Related causative patterns with distinct lexical selection.

patterns.form: make/let + person + bare infinitive; help + person + (to-)infinitive
patterns.meaning: Complement patterns depend on the selected verb and meaning.

examples.sentence: We had the locks changed after the move.
examples.analysis: The subject arranged the service; the sentence does not identify the worker.

examples.sentence: The noise made the lecturer pause.
examples.analysis: Make introduces the person affected and the bare infinitive pause.

examples.sentence: The assistant helped the visitor to complete the form.
examples.analysis: To complete is standard after help; complete without to would also be standard.

contrasts.note: Both grammatical; the first is past perfect with us as repairers in the ordinary reading, while the second normally describes an arranged service.

exceptions: Have an object stolen can report an unwanted experience rather than deliberate causation. Help admits infinitives with or without to. Fixed be let go is not evidence for unrestricted passive permission constructions.

mistakes.problem: The supervisor made us to wait.
mistakes.reason: Active causative make takes a bare infinitive here.

mistakes.repair: We were made to wait outside.
mistakes.reason: Passive make uses the to-infinitive in this construction.

glossary.definition: A construction expressing causing, arranging or enabling an event.
An infinitival verb form without to.
glossary.example: In They let us leave, leave is bare.

modules.title: Passivisation limits, ergative alternation and meaning
modules.definition: Passivisation depends on a licensed verb-and-complement pattern; an ergative alternation instead uses the same lexical verb transitively for causing a change and intransitively for the change itself.
foundation: Some active clauses have no object available for the ordinary passive operation: The parcel arrived; the children slept. The parcel was arrived is not the standard passive equivalent of arrived. A subject complement after a linking verb is not a direct object: She became a doctor cannot be mechanically turned into A doctor was become by her. These restrictions follow from the construction, not from whether the event seems important or whether the subject is human. First identify objects and complements, then ask whether the lexical verb supports the intended passive.
intermediate: English also permits some prepositional passives: Someone looked into the complaint can correspond to The complaint was looked into. The preposition remains with the verb, even though the complaint is now subject. The bed has been slept in is another established example. Such constructions show why only verbs with a direct object can ever be passive is too broad. They do not mean that every prepositional phrase can be promoted naturally; lexical restrictions, idiomatic units and the relationship of the affected participant to the event matter. A learner's dictionary and established usage help resolve difficult individual cases.
advanced: Many change-of-state verbs alternate: Heat cracked the glass; The glass cracked. In the first, heat is a cause and glass an object; in the second, glass is subject in an active intransitive clause. The glass was cracked by the heat is passive and expresses the cause differently. The active intransitive does not identify an external cause and must not be described as passive merely because its subject undergoes a change. Open, break, melt and increase permit comparable patterns in suitable senses, but not all transitive verbs alternate: A thief stole the bag does not license The bag stole with the same meaning.
expert: Meaning-preserving transformations require a final interpretation check. The scope of negation, quantifiers and modals can change when information is rearranged: Not every file was checked denies complete checking. Every file was not checked can be scope-ambiguous; use No file was checked for an explicit zero-checking claim. Keep a specific agent when that agent is part of the original informational task, preserve tense and aspect, and avoid changing an unsuccessful attempt into a completed event. Some stative transitive verbs have limited or unusual passives in ordinary senses; an awkward example is not automatically a universal ban on the verb. Distinguish syntactic possibility, normal collocation and discourse usefulness, and explain precisely which restriction an exercise intends to test.

patterns.form: cause + transitive change verb + affected object
patterns.meaning: A causative active use, such as heat melted the wax.
An active intransitive alternation, such as the wax melted.

patterns.form: promoted subject + be + past participle + retained preposition (+ by-agent)
patterns.meaning: A licensed prepositional passive retains the preposition selected by the verb, as in The matter was looked into.

examples.analysis: Rise is intransitive here; no ordinary object can become a passive subject.

examples.sentence: The complaint was looked into by an independent reviewer.
examples.analysis: A prepositional passive retains into and identifies the reviewer.

examples.sentence: The window opened when the latch loosened.
examples.analysis: Opened is active intransitive, even though window undergoes the change.

contrasts.note: Both grammatical active clauses; the second leaves the cause unexpressed and is not a passive transformation by form alone.

exceptions: Some clauses without a direct object permit prepositional passives. An affected subject does not by itself make a clause passive. Stative verbs require sense-specific and usage-sensitive analysis.

mistakes.problem: The parcel was arrived before noon.
mistakes.reason: Arrive does not form the intended be-passive.

mistakes.problem: The complaint was looked by an investigator into.
mistakes.repair: The complaint was looked into by an investigator.
mistakes.reason: Keep the verb-preposition unit in its normal passive order before the agent phrase.

glossary.definition: A pedagogical label for a transitive causative and related active intransitive change-of-state pair.
glossary.example: The sun melted the snow / The snow melted.

glossary.definition: A passive related to a verb-plus-preposition construction.
glossary.example: That problem has been dealt with.

questions.prompt: Keep the ongoing present reading: “The technician is repairing the scanner” → “The scanner ____ by the technician.”
questions.why: Is being repaired preserves present progressive aspect and changes voice.

questions.prompt: Complete the perfect passive: “The letters have been ____.”
questions.why: Passive be requires the lexical participle written.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is a passive infinitive?
questions.why: To be checked contains infinitival be plus the lexical participle.

questions.prompt: A report says “The manuscript is believed to have survived the fire.” What does that form establish?
options: Survival is attributed as a belief, with earlier time reference.
The sentence proves survival beyond doubt.
The fire will necessarily occur tomorrow.
Believed must be replaced by believing.
questions.why: The construction reports a belief and uses the perfect infinitive for an earlier event; attribution is not proof.

questions.prompt: Which statement about “She got promoted” is accurate?
options: Got promoted is automatically an adjective before a noun.
Get-passives can describe a positive event.
questions.why: Get-passives are not confined to undesirable outcomes and do not by themselves assign blame.

questions.prompt: Use active causative make: “The interruption made us ____ again.”
questions.why: Active causative make selects object plus bare infinitive start.

questions.prompt: Which pair consists of two standard help constructions?
options: help me checks / help me checking
help me check / help me to check
help me checking / help me checked
help to me check / help me to checking
questions.why: Help accepts an object followed by an infinitive with or without to.

questions.prompt: Inspect: “The visitors were made to wait outside.”
options: to must be deleted after passive made
questions.why: Passive made takes to wait; plural visitors agrees with were.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an established prepositional passive?
options: The visitor was became a member.
questions.why: Look into permits this prepositional passive; the other verbs do not form the proposed passives in these uses.

questions.prompt: In “The ice melted”, which analysis is correct?
options: Passive solely because ice is affected
Passive perfect because melted ends in -ed
A causative clause with an expressed agent
questions.why: The clause has an active intransitive verb; an affected subject alone does not establish passive voice.

questions.prompt: Make passive, retaining the agent: “Nora checked the figures.”
questions.model: The figures were checked by Nora.
rubric: Promote figures and use were checked.
Retain Nora as the expressed agent.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Supply the missing auxiliaries: “The forms have ____ checked and may ____ approved tomorrow.”
rubric: Use perfect been before the first participle.
Use base be after modal may.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Analyse the chain in “The bridge will have been inspected by Friday”.
questions.model: Will is the finite modal, have marks the perfect, been is passive be, and inspected is the lexical participle.
rubric: Identify each auxiliary’s role.
Retain the deadline reference.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Why is “has been being repaired” normally recast rather than automatically called impossible?
questions.model: It is a possible perfect-progressive passive but uncommon and heavy; an active or contextual alternative is often easier to process.
rubric: Distinguish grammatical availability from preference.
Preserve the continuation/duration meaning in any suggested recast.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Use a recipient passive: “The charity gave the school a printer.”
questions.model: The school was given a printer by the charity.
rubric: Promote the recipient school.
Retain printer and the stated donor.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Express the same transfer with printer as subject: “The charity gave the school a printer.”
questions.model: A printer was given to the school by the charity.
rubric: Promote the transferred item.
Use to for the recipient in this pattern.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Compare “The door was closed at six” as an event report and as a state description.
questions.model: An event reading reports the closing at six; a state reading says the door was in the closed state then. Context, not the ending alone, resolves the reading.
rubric: Describe both readings.
Do not claim every be-plus-participle sequence has one analysis.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain what is lost when “The appeal panel overturned the decision” becomes simply “The decision was overturned”.
questions.model: The passive leaves the agent unexpressed; the original specifically identifies the appeal panel.
rubric: Identify the omitted participant.
Do not invent an alternative agent.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain “We had repaired the scanner” versus “We had the scanner repaired”.
questions.model: The first is past perfect, ordinarily describing our repair; the second normally says we arranged for someone to repair it.
rubric: Distinguish auxiliary have from object-plus-participle have.
Keep the difference in participant roles.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Use get + person + to-infinitive: “We persuaded the technician to check the wiring.”
questions.model: We got the technician to check the wiring.
rubric: Use technician as the object of get.
Retain the intended cooperative/persuasive reading.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Why does “They had their car stolen” not normally mean they arranged theft?
questions.model: The have-object-participle construction can report an unwanted experience affecting the subject; context supplies that reading.
rubric: Recognise the adverse-experience pattern.
Do not infer deliberate causation from form alone.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Give the ordinary passive permission alternative: “The supervisor let us leave.”
questions.model: We were allowed to leave by the supervisor.
rubric: Use be allowed to for the stated permission sense.
Retain the source of permission.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Classify voice and transitivity: “The heat cracked the glass” / “The glass cracked” / “The glass was cracked by the heat”.
rubric: Use construction, not affectedness alone.
Identify the change in expression of cause and affected participant.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Why is “The bed has been slept in” relevant to the rule “Only direct-object verbs can have passives”?
questions.model: It is an established prepositional passive related to someone sleeping in the bed; the absolute rule is too broad.
rubric: Identify the retained preposition.
Limit the conclusion to licensed constructions rather than every prepositional phrase.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Why cannot “She became a doctor” be converted mechanically to “A doctor was become by her”?
questions.model: Doctor is a subject complement after linking became, not the object required for that proposed passive operation.
rubric: Identify the complement’s function.
Distinguish it from a direct object.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Revise the analysis: “The window opened. This is passive because the window received an action. All verbs describing affected things are passive.”
questions.model: The window opened is active intransitive. Its subject undergoes a change, but passive voice is a grammatical construction, not a synonym for affectedness.
rubric: Correct both false generalisations.
Keep the original event description unchanged.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Explain “Not every file was checked” versus “Every file was not checked”.
questions.model: The first denies complete checking and allows some checked files. The second is scope-ambiguous in ordinary use and may be understood as none checked; rewrite explicitly if that is intended.
rubric: Identify the partial-negative meaning of not every.
Avoid treating the second wording as a uniquely reliable paraphrase.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

questions.prompt: Write an active and passive version of a notice that names who will inspect the lift tomorrow.
questions.model: A qualified engineer will inspect the lift tomorrow. / The lift will be inspected tomorrow by a qualified engineer.
rubric: Keep future time and the named agent class.
Explain which information each version places first.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the intended participants and time: The records have been wrote.
rubric: Use the lexical participle written.
Accept equivalent grammatical repairs that do not invent an agent or alter modality.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the intended participants and time: The report may been published tomorrow.
corrections.model: The report may be published tomorrow.
rubric: Use base be after may.
Accept equivalent grammatical repairs that do not invent an agent or alter modality.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the intended participants and time: She was explained the new rule.
corrections.model: The new rule was explained to her.
rubric: Follow the ordinary explain-something-to-someone pattern.
Accept equivalent grammatical repairs that do not invent an agent or alter modality.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the intended participants and time: The archive is believed to opened in 1980.
corrections.model: The archive is believed to have opened in 1980.
rubric: Use a perfect infinitive for the earlier opening.
Accept equivalent grammatical repairs that do not invent an agent or alter modality.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the intended participants and time: The supervisor made us to sign.
rubric: Active causative make selects a bare infinitive.
Accept equivalent grammatical repairs that do not invent an agent or alter modality.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the intended participants and time: We were made sign.
rubric: Passive make uses a to-infinitive.
Accept equivalent grammatical repairs that do not invent an agent or alter modality.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the intended participants and time: She helped me to check the invoice.
rubric: Help permits an infinitive with to as well as without it.
Accept equivalent grammatical repairs that do not invent an agent or alter modality.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if needed, preserving the intended participants and time: The parcel was arrived before lunch.
rubric: Arrive is intransitive in this use and has no intended be-passive.
Accept equivalent grammatical repairs that do not invent an agent or alter modality.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

transformations.prompt: Make passive while retaining every stated participant and the perfect aspect: “The registrar has approved the application.”
transformations.model: The application has been approved by the registrar.
rubric: Use has been approved.
Retain the registrar as agent and application as affected participant.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

transformations.prompt: Use have + object + participle while preserving the arrangement: “Yesterday we arranged for a mechanic to service the van on Friday.”
transformations.model: Yesterday we arranged to have the van serviced by a mechanic on Friday.
rubric: Use have + van + serviced within the arrangement.
Preserve yesterday as arrangement time and Friday as the planned service time; do not assert completion.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

writing.prompt: Write a 100–140-word maintenance update containing an active clause with a named agent, an agentless passive, a reporting passive and a causative service arrangement. Explain why each wording fits the information needed.
writing.model:
A qualified engineer inspected the lift on Monday and identified wear in one cable. The lift has been taken out of service while replacement parts are obtained. The building is believed to have used the same control system for more than fifteen years, although the installation record has not yet been found. We have arranged to have the cable replaced by an authorised contractor, but the repair is not yet complete. During the closure, staff will help visitors reach services on the ground floor. The contractor will confirm a service date after inspecting the replacement part. We will issue another update when a reopening time is available.

Analysis: The active names the engineer; the agentless passive focuses on service status. The reporting passive qualifies a historical belief. Arranged to have…replaced describes a service arrangement, not a completed repair.
rubric: Include the four specified constructions accurately.
Distinguish attributed belief from confirmed fact.
Preserve clear responsibility where the context needs it.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 8: does “has been checked” necessarily mean the same time relationship as “was checked yesterday”?
recall.model: No. The former is present perfect with a passive; the latter locates the event in a specified completed past time.
rubric: Identify both aspect/time choices.
Do not infer identical discourse use from a shared participle.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 17: identify modal form requirements in “The visitors must be allowed to leave”.
recall.model: Must takes base be; passive allowed takes the to-infinitive leave in the permission construction.
rubric: Identify the two different selection relationships.
Do not delete every to merely because a modal occurs earlier.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 14: in “The room was repaired because the roof leaked”, identify main and reason clauses.
recall.model: The room was repaired is the main clause; because the roof leaked is the subordinate reason clause.
rubric: Identify clause boundaries.
Keep leaked outside the passive chain was repaired.
alternatives: Other answers are acceptable if they preserve the stated meaning and meet the listed structural requirements.

checklist: I preserve tense, aspect and modal meaning in a passive.
I explain agent omission without inventing responsibility.
I distinguish arranged causation from an adverse experience.
I recognise licensed prepositional passives and active intransitive changes.
I check every transformation for lost or strengthened meaning.
